title: Education
author: Firth, Jonathan
summary: Jonathan Firth addresses the question of whether classroom teachers can meaningfully participate in educational research, not just as subjects or consumers of evidence but as contributors to the knowledge base. Firth distinguishes three modes of teacher research engagement: consuming published research and translating it into practice, implementing evidence-based approaches in ways that constitute systematic inquiry, and contributing original data or analysis to the broader field. The essay is grounded in realistic constraints teachers face including limited time, minimal institutional support, and the gap between academic publication norms and classroom practice, while arguing these constraints do not disqualify teachers from research but require honesty about what kind is achievable. Firth argues the gap between academic and practitioner knowledge is narrowed most when teachers engage seriously with existing research even when they cannot produce it themselves. The Learning Scientists and similar networks represent viable models for practitioners who want a disciplined relationship with the evidence base without requiring the infrastructure of academic research.
points: Firth distinguishes three meaningful forms of teacher-researcher engagement: consuming and translating published evidence, implementing evidence-based practices as systematic inquiry, and contributing original data, each legitimate and each requiring different conditions.

The research-practice gap in education is partly a translation problem, and teachers who engage seriously with research literature are among the most effective translators between what scientists find and what classrooms do.
Time constraints on teachers are real limitations on original research production but do not prevent the intellectually rigorous engagement with evidence that most directly improves student outcomes.

Teacher engagement with existing research is often more practically valuable than teacher-led original research: a teacher who can evaluate and implement a meta-analysis contributes more to student outcomes than one who collects data but cannot assess the existing evidence base.

The Learning Scientists network represents a viable model for teacher-researcher engagement: practitioners who maintain a disciplined relationship with the evidence base without requiring academic institutional infrastructure.
quotes: A few of the updates I've shared recently connect in some way to how educators engage with research evidence. I'm interested in how we act as (sceptical) consumers of research, how we stay open to adjusting our own ideas as we learn more about the evidence. I'm also very curious about what role teachers play in doing and sharing research.

I suppose I saw psychology research and teaching as two rather different worlds. Like a lot of new teachers, my practice was probably heavily influenced by tradition and by my own experiences, as well as by some of the fads policies of the time! It was only when I began to get frustrated by practical issues such as forgetting and student underperformance that I began to look deeper into ideas like long-term memory and the spacing effect, and saw how potentially transformative these could be.

Recommended talk on the issue The fascinating talk below by Tracey Tokuhama-Espinosa, shared with the Centre for Educational Neuroscience a few months ago, reflects well on these issues and comes from someone who has studied the issue of teacher research engagement. The title is, 'How can teachers become learning scientists, and why would this improve education?'.

Engagement in and with research Being a teacher and a learning scientist could mean different things. It could involve: Engagement with research, reading it and trying to apply it; Sharing ideas and influencing practice to become Page 1 more evidence-based; Carrying out your own research. Where are you in the process of engagement with and in research?

If not, perhaps that could be something to explore in the next academic year. Tokuhama-Espinosa if you want to find out more about her work in this area: Tokuhama-Espinosa, T., & Nouri, A. Teachers' mind, brain, and education literacy: A survey of scientists' views.
